source.title: Scaling Laws Under the Microscope: Predicting Transformer Performance from Small Scale Experiments
source.authors: Maor Ivgi; Y. Carmon; Jonathan Berant

record.tranche_reason: The study measures parameter-scaling fits and extrapolation, then shows that downstream fits vary by task and are sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and convergence. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports pretraining evaluation-loss fits, finetuning task fits and predictions, and tuning/convergence effects. It does not test a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Several task metrics and prediction results are reported separately; rows below retain those results. The 85M pretraining model was excluded from the fit and used to assess extrapolation.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to pretraining loss (MLM/PMI encoders, about 10K–6M params) and to finetuned task metrics on 9 tasks. It tests extrapolation to BERT-Base and shows the fits depend on task, metric, per-scale hyperparameter tuning, smallest-scale inclusion and convergence. These are qualifying results on V1, V2, V4, V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find near-perfect pretraining-loss power laws for both objectives and both aspect ratios. At finetuning, scaling laws emerge only for some tasks, possibly those close to the LM objective with ample data. When fit R²≥0.95, fits predict a ~10x larger model well and allow model selection, and they also help debug convergence. Per-scale HPT and careful convergence are needed, which partly offsets the claimed 2.5–5x compute savings.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parameter-count scaling and log-log power-law fitting for language-model evaluation loss, but studies small encoder-only MLM/PMI models and downstream finetuning metrics rather than the original broad parameter/data/compute sweeps. It uses bootstrap fit uncertainty and explicitly tests prediction utility.
record.method_sensitivity: Finetuning task and metric, pretraining objective, aspect ratio, per-scale hyperparameter tuning, minimum model size, and pretraining early-stopping patience/convergence.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 2022
record.problems: The pretraining sweep has a single random seed; finetuning uses five seeds. The largest model is suspected to be undertrained, predictions are limited to one BERT-Base model and roughly an order-of-magnitude scale increase, and the authors state they lack empirical evidence for significantly larger or decoder-based models. Fit quality is poor or non-monotonic on some tasks.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, repeated aggregate presentations of fit statistics already represented by the objective-specific rows, some predicted-versus-actual task values in App. A.5 Table 7, and secondary explanatory discussion were not given additional rows. The paper's separate evaluation-loss fits during finetuning are explicitly described as not tested for scaling laws (§4.1, App. A.6), so they are not recorded as test results.

untested.parts: Scaling in data tokens or compute; decoder/autoregressive LMs; parameter ranges beyond about 10K–6M (single pretraining seed).
Pretraining-loss extrapolation over multiple orders of magnitude; only one 14x-larger model is tested.
Entire version: no compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
Shapes other than aspect ratios 32 and 64; other architecture details.
Other modalities, repeated data, transfer scaling in data; decoder models; non-English tasks.
Generation tasks, larger models, and prediction from pretraining loss rather than parameter count.
Parameter counting conventions, training schedules, compute-optimal split disagreements.

missing.what: R²_2: (fit excluding 1-layer models) changes goodness-of-fit and prediction error. SQuAD 2.0 0.797→0.917, RACE 0.916→0.974, MRPC 0.763→0.849; BoolQ drops to 0.669. RE_2: improves for these tasks. This is a fitting choice that changes results.
Pretraining runs that early-stopped had loss above the fit; raising patience brought them to the predicted value.
Fitting finetuning eval loss instead of the target metric lowers R² by over 10% on average.
Hierarchical vs naive bootstrap gives wider slope CIs (e.g. RACE [−0.07,−0.04] vs [−0.06,−0.04]). Shows uncertainty depends on fitting method.
PMI-pretrained BERT-Base predicted vs actual and RE_2: per task

record.verdict_notes: The pretraining sweep uses a single seed, and the pretraining loss is masked-LM loss of encoders, not autoregressive loss. The V5/V6 split: finetuned task-metric scaling is linked to both. HPT rows were moved to V7 only, because the base fits already appear in R6–R23. Wrong-sign model-selection rows were recoded from reversed to absent.

versions.untested_parts: Tests evaluation loss versus parameter count for pretraining objectives; does not test variation in training tokens or compute, or independently establish several orders of magnitude for each.

Tests extrapolation of pretraining evaluation loss to one larger model, and downstream task performance predictions to larger models; does not test pretraining-loss extrapolation over multiple orders of magnitude.
Compares two aspect ratios in pretraining; does not test a wide range of architectures or isolate depth and width at fixed parameter count.
Tests scaling fits during English encoder-model finetuning on nine understanding tasks; does not test other modalities, repeated data, or transfer regimes beyond these tasks.
Tests downstream task-metric predictions from parameter-scaling fits; does not establish general predictability across tasks or generated-language capabilities.

Shows sensitivity to finetuning hyperparameter tuning, task/metric, model size threshold, and convergence. Does not test compute-optimal allocation disagreements or comprehensively compare fitting methods.
